lessons.title: Fabric Selection: Cotton, Bamboo, and Microfiber
lessons.body:
Choosing the right fabrics is the first step to making a reusable pad that is comfortable, absorbent, and long-lasting. The top layer that touches the skin should be soft and breathable. Cotton is the best choice: it is cool, allows air to flow, and does not irritate the skin. Look for 100% cotton, preferably unbleached or naturally dyed. Flannel cotton is also good because it is soft and absorbent. Bamboo is another option; it is very soft, naturally antibacterial, and more absorbent than cotton. However, bamboo can be more expensive and harder to find in local markets. Microfiber is a synthetic fabric that absorbs liquid quickly and holds it well, but it should not be used directly against the skin because it can cause irritation and does not breathe. Instead, use microfiber as an inner absorbent layer.

For the core absorbent layers, you need fabrics that soak up liquid fast and hold it without leaking. Cotton fleece, bamboo fleece, or microfiber terry are excellent. You can also use old towels or flannel sheets, but make sure they are clean and not worn thin. For the waterproof backing, you need a fabric that stops liquid from passing through. Polyurethane laminate (PUL) is the best choice: it is thin, waterproof, and breathable. Alternatively, you can use a waterproof nylon or polyester fabric, but PUL is more comfortable. Avoid plastic sheets as they do not breathe and can cause rashes.

When buying fabrics, always wash them first to shrink them and remove any chemicals. Pre-washing also makes the fabric softer. In Africa, you can find suitable fabrics at local markets, fabric shops, or online suppliers. Cotton and bamboo are often sold as meters or yards. For a single reusable pad, you need about 20 cm by 30 cm of each fabric type. A typical pad has three layers: a soft top layer, one or two absorbent layers, and a waterproof backing. You can add more absorbent layers for heavy flow. Always test a small piece of fabric by dropping water on it to see how quickly it absorbs and whether it leaks through. This simple test saves you from making pads that fail.

lessons.title: Pattern Making and Sizing
lessons.body:
A pattern is a template you use to cut fabric into the shape of a pad. You can make patterns from cardboard, old X-ray film, or thick plastic. Start by drawing the shape of a pad on paper. A standard reusable pad is about 24 cm long and 8 cm wide at the center, with wings that extend 4 cm on each side. For heavy flow, make it longer (28 cm) and wider (10 cm). For light flow or panty liners, use 18 cm by 6 cm. You can also make different sizes for day and night. Remember that the pad should fit comfortably in the underwear without bunching.

To make a pattern, draw half the pad shape on a folded piece of paper, then cut it out and unfold it to get a symmetrical shape. Use a ruler to keep lines straight. For the wings, draw curves that will wrap around the underwear. You can add a snap or button later. Once you have a paper pattern, trace it onto your chosen pattern material. Cut it out carefully. Label the pattern with the size and the type of fabric (e.g., 'Top layer', 'Absorbent', 'Backing').

When cutting fabric, place the pattern on the fabric and pin it down. Use sharp scissors or a rotary cutter. Cut two pieces for the top layer (if you want a folded edge) and two for the backing, plus one or two absorbent layers. Always cut on the grain of the fabric to prevent stretching. If you are making many pads, you can stack fabric layers and cut multiple pieces at once. But be careful to keep the pattern aligned.

Sizing is important for comfort and leak protection. Measure the underwear you will wear with the pad. The pad should be long enough to cover the crotch area and extend a little at the front and back. The wings should be long enough to wrap around the gusset and snap together. Test the pattern by making a sample pad with cheap fabric first. Wear it for a few hours to see if it fits well. Adjust the pattern as needed. In Africa, many women prefer pads that are not too bulky, so keep the absorbent layers thin but effective. You can also make patterns for different flow levels and offer them as a set.

lessons.title: Sewing and Assembly Techniques
lessons.body:
Sewing a reusable pad requires a basic sewing machine or a needle and thread if you are hand-sewing. A sewing machine makes the work faster and stronger. Use a straight stitch for most seams and a zigzag stitch for edges to prevent fraying. If you have a serger, it is ideal for finishing edges. Start by sewing the absorbent layers together. Stack one or two absorbent layers (e.g., cotton fleece) and sew them along the edges with a zigzag stitch. This keeps them from shifting. If you want extra absorbency, you can quilt the layers by sewing lines across them.

Next, attach the absorbent layer to the waterproof backing. Place the backing with the shiny side (waterproof side) down, and the absorbent layer on top. Pin them together. Sew around the edges with a straight stitch, leaving a small opening (about 5 cm) on one side so you can turn the pad inside out. Trim the corners to reduce bulk. Then turn the pad right side out through the opening. Use a blunt tool like a chopstick to push out the corners. Press the pad flat with an iron on low heat (be careful with PUL; do not iron directly).

Now attach the top layer. The top layer should be slightly larger than the pad so you can fold it over the edges. Place the top layer over the absorbent side, right sides together. Sew around the entire pad, leaving a gap for turning. Turn it right side out and sew the opening closed with a slip stitch or topstitch. For a neat finish, topstitch around the entire pad 3 mm from the edge. This also secures all layers.

Finally, add the wings. Cut wing pieces from the top fabric and backing. Sew them to the sides of the pad, reinforcing with a zigzag stitch. You can also add a snap or Velcro to the wings for fastening. Test the pad by pulling gently on the seams to ensure they are strong. Remember to backstitch at the beginning and end of every seam. If you are hand-sewing, use a backstitch for strength. Always use polyester thread because it is strong and durable. Cotton thread can break easily. Keep your stitches small and even for a professional look.

lessons.title: Insertion of Absorbent Layers
lessons.body:
The absorbent layers are the heart of a reusable pad. They determine how much liquid the pad can hold and how dry the top layer feels. You can use natural fabrics like cotton, bamboo, or hemp, or synthetic microfiber. For a typical pad, you need 2 to 4 layers of absorbent fabric, depending on the flow. For light flow, use 2 layers; for heavy flow, use 4 layers. Each layer should be cut to the same shape as the pad body, but slightly smaller so they fit inside the pad without sticking out.

When inserting absorbent layers, you can either sew them directly into the pad or make them removable. Sewn-in layers are simpler and less likely to shift. To sew them in, stack the layers on top of the waterproof backing, then cover with the top layer and sew all around. Removable layers are inserted into a pocket, which makes drying faster and allows you to adjust absorbency. To make a pocket, sew the top layer and backing together leaving one end open, then insert the absorbent layers. You can also make separate absorbent inserts that you place inside the pocket. This is useful for heavy flow days when you need extra protection.

If you use microfiber, place it in the middle, not against the skin. Microfiber absorbs quickly but can cause irritation if it touches the skin. Also, microfiber can be bulky, so use it sparingly. Natural fibers like cotton and bamboo are more breathable and comfortable against the skin. You can combine fabrics: a layer of microfiber for quick absorption, then a layer of cotton for holding liquid. This gives you the best of both.

Before sewing, test the absorbency of your layers by pouring a small amount of water (about 30 ml) onto them. See how quickly it absorbs and whether it leaks through. If it leaks, add more layers or use a more absorbent fabric. Also, consider the drying time. More layers take longer to dry, especially in humid climates. In Africa, where sun drying is common, thinner layers dry faster and are less likely to develop mold. Always wash and dry absorbent layers thoroughly before use. You can also pre-shrink them by washing in hot water and drying on high heat. This prevents the pad from shrinking after sewing.

lessons.title: Finishing and Fastening Methods
lessons.body:
Finishing touches make your reusable pad look professional and function well. After sewing all layers, you need to secure the edges and add fastening. The most common fastening is a snap button, but you can also use Velcro (hook and loop tape) or even buttons and buttonholes. Snaps are durable, easy to use, and do not snag. You can buy snap pliers and snap sets from craft shops or online. To attach a snap, you need to make a small hole in the wing, then press the snap parts together with the pliers. Alternatively, you can sew on snaps by hand. Velcro is cheaper and easier to find, but it can wear out over time and may catch on other fabrics in the wash. If you use Velcro, sew the hook side on one wing and the loop side on the other.

Another finishing method is to add a layer of topstitching around the entire pad. This reinforces the edges and gives a neat look. Use a contrasting thread color if you like. You can also add a decorative stitch, but keep it functional. For the wings, you can shape them into a curve that wraps around the underwear. Make sure the wings are long enough to overlap by at least 2 cm when fastened. Test the fastening by putting the pad on underwear and adjusting the fit. The pad should stay in place without shifting.

If you are making pads for sale, consider adding a label with care instructions. You can sew a small tag on the back with washing symbols. Also, consider the color and pattern of the top fabric. Dark colors hide stains better, but light colors show if the pad is clean. Many women prefer dark or patterned fabrics for the top layer. For the backing, you can use a solid color. You can also add a layer of fleece or flannel on the back for extra softness against the underwear.

Finally, trim any loose threads and check all seams. A well-finished pad should have no raw edges that can fray. If you do not have a serger, use a zigzag stitch or fold the edges over and stitch. For a truly professional finish, you can bind the edges with bias tape. This is a strip of fabric that you sew around the edge. It adds durability and a nice look. Practice on scrap fabric until you are confident. Remember, the goal is a pad that is comfortable, leak-proof, and easy to wash.

lessons.title: Quality Checks for Reusable Pads
lessons.body:
Quality checks ensure that every reusable pad you make is safe, effective, and durable. Start by inspecting the fabric before cutting. Look for holes, stains, or weak spots. Do not use damaged fabric. After cutting, check that all pieces are the correct size and shape. A simple ruler check saves time later. When sewing, check the seams as you go. Pull gently on the seam to see if it holds. If it opens, reinforce with a second stitch. Also, check for skipped stitches or loose threads. A good seam is tight and even.

After assembly, test the pad for absorbency. Pour 30 ml of water (about two tablespoons) onto the center of the pad. It should absorb within 30 seconds without leaking through the backing. If it pools on the surface, the absorbent layers are not working. You may need to add more layers or change the fabric. Also, check the waterproof backing by placing a tissue under the pad and pressing. If the tissue gets wet, the backing is not waterproof. In that case, use a different backing or add another layer of PUL.

Check the fastening. Snap or Velcro should hold securely but be easy to open. Test by fastening and unfastening five times. If it loosens, replace it. Check the wings: they should be long enough to wrap around the underwear and overlap. The pad should not shift when you walk or sit. You can test by wearing the pad for an hour with a light flow or with water. Also, check for comfort: no scratchy edges, no bulky areas. The pad should feel soft against the skin.

Finally, wash the pad according to instructions and check for shrinkage or damage. A good pad should survive at least 50 washes. After washing, check that the layers have not separated and that the waterproof backing is still intact. If you are selling pads, establish a quality control checklist. For example: 1) All seams are secure. 2) Pad absorbs 30 ml in 30 seconds. 3) No leaks through backing. 4) Fasteners work. 5) No loose threads. 6) Correct size. 7) Comfortable to wear. Keep records of your checks. This helps you maintain consistent quality and build trust with customers. Remember, a high-quality pad protects the user and the environment.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Manufacturing Reusable Sanitary Pads in Africa

This practical reference consolidates the core technical knowledge from the Manufacturing Processes for Reusable Pads module. It is designed for trainers, production supervisors, and entrepreneurs running small- to medium-scale pad-making enterprises in Africa. The focus is on repeatable, low-cost, high-quality production that meets real market demand â because in this business, product performance drives repeat sales, and repeat sales drive profit.

Across sub-Saharan Africa, reusable pad enterprises operate at very different scales â from 5-unit-per-day home workshops to 500-unit-per-day semi-industrial facilities. The principles below apply at every level, but the equipment, batch sizes, and quality tolerances must be adapted to your actual production capacity and target market (schoolgirls, NGOs, retail pharmacies, or export buyers).

1. Fabric Selection: Matching Material to Market

Fabric choice is the single biggest driver of both production cost and product performance. In African markets, you must balance three factors: absorbency, breathability, and local availability. Imported microfiber may outperform local cotton, but if it doubles your unit cost and adds 6 weeks to your supply chain, it may not be the right choice for your business model.

Table 1: Fabric Comparison for Reusable Pad Production
Fabric Best Use Absorbency Cost (USD/m) African Availability
Cotton jersey (100%) Top layer (wicking) LowâMedium $2.50â$4.00 High (local mills in Kenya, Nigeria, Egypt)
Bamboo terry Absorbent core High $4.00â$7.00 LowâMedium (imported from China/India)
Microfiber (80/20 poly-polyamide) Absorbent core Very High $3.00â$5.50 Medium (imported, available in bulk)
PUL (polyurethane laminate) Waterproof barrier None (barrier) $5.00â$9.00 Low (imported; some suppliers in South Africa)
Cotton flannel Outer backing Low $2.00â$3.50 High (local textile markets)

Sources: Days for Girls International (2021) Reusable Pad Production Manual; UNHCR (2019) Menstrual Hygiene Management Guide; market prices surveyed in Nairobi, Lagos, and Accra (2024).

2. Pattern Making and Sizing

Pattern accuracy determines fit, comfort, and leakage prevention. A pad that slips or bunches will not be repurchased, no matter how good the fabric. Standard African market sizes are:

  • Regular (Day): 24â26 cm long, 7â8 cm wide at center, wings 5â6 cm
  • Night/Heavy: 30â34 cm long, 8â9 cm wide at center, extended back coverage
  • Teen/Small: 20â22 cm long, 6â7 cm wide (for schoolgirl programs)

Use cardboard or plastic template patterns and trace with tailor's chalk. Always cut with the grain of the fabric to minimize stretching. For production runs above 50 units, invest in acrylic or metal templates â they last years and reduce cutting errors by up to 30%.

3. Sewing and Assembly Techniques

Assembly order matters. The standard production sequence is:

  1. Cut all layers to pattern
  2. Sew absorbent core layers together (zigzag or overlock)
  3. Stack: top layer â core â PUL â backing
  4. Pin or clip all layers
  5. Sew around the perimeter with 1 cm seam allowance
  6. Turn inside out (if using the "bag" method) or bind edges
  7. Topstitch 2â3 mm from edge for durability
  8. Attach fasteners (snaps or Velcro)

Use a ballpoint needle (size 80/12) for knit fabrics and a universal needle (size 90/14) for woven. Polyester thread (40-weight) is the standard for African production â it resists moisture and holds up to repeated washing better than cotton thread.

4. Insertion of Absorbent Layers

Absorbent capacity is the most common failure point in reusable pads. A pad that leaks after 2 hours is not a reusable pad â it is a complaint waiting to happen. Target capacity:

  • Regular pad: 30â40 ml total capacity
  • Night pad: 45â60 ml total capacity

Microfiber holds roughly 5â7 times its weight in water; bamboo terry holds 3â4 times. For a 40 ml pad, use 2 layers of microfiber (approximately 60 g total) or 3 layers of bamboo terry. Always pre-wash absorbent fabrics before cutting â they shrink 5â10% and pre-washing prevents post-sale shrinkage complaints.

5. Finishing and Fastening Methods

Finishing determines whether your pad looks professional or homemade. Key steps:

  • Edge binding: Use bias tape or fold-over elastic for a clean finish. This adds 8â12 minutes per pad but reduces fraying and extends product life.
  • Fasteners: Snap buttons (plastic or metal) are preferred in most African markets â they last longer than Velcro, do not snag on underwear, and are quieter. Velcro is cheaper but degrades after 50â80 washes.
  • Wing placement: Wings should be positioned 2â3 cm from the center on each side, angled slightly downward for secure wrapping.

6. Quality Checks for Reusable Pads

Quality control is not optional if you want repeat customers. Implement a 3-stage check: incoming fabric inspection, in-process checks, and final product testing.

Table 2: Quality Control Checklist and Tolerances
Check Point Standard Test Method Defect Action
Seam integrity No gaps, no loose threads Visual + pull test (2 kg) Re-sew or reject
Absorbency 30â40 ml (regular) Pour 40 ml water, wait 60 sec Add core layer or reject
Waterproof barrier No leakage after 40 ml Place on tissue, pour water Check PUL placement
Fastener function Snap closes securely, 100+ cycles Open/close 20 times Replace fastener
Size accuracy Â±0.5 cm of pattern Measure with tape Re-cut if outside tolerance
Shrinkage (after wash) <5% length change Wash 3x at 60Â°C, measure Pre-wash fabric next batch

Sources: WHO/UNICEF (2012) Consultation on Draft Long List of Indicators for MHM; Days for Girls International (2021); field testing data from Ugandan and Kenyan production units (2023).

â  SAFETY WARNING â Heat and Chemical Hazards

When using PUL (polyurethane laminate), do not iron directly â PUL melts at approximately 140Â°C and releases toxic fumes. Use a pressing cloth and low heat, or avoid ironing PUL entirely. When handling microfiber, wash hands after contact to avoid transferring oils that reduce absorbency. If using industrial sewing machines, ensure proper needle guards and eye protection are in place. Never use bleach or fabric softener during pre-washing â both damage absorbent fibers and reduce pad performance. Store finished pads in a dry, dust-free area away from direct sunlight to prevent PUL degradation.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Pre-wash all absorbent fabrics (cotton, bamboo, microfiber) before cutting to prevent shrinkage.
  2. Cut with grain and use templates for consistent sizing across batches.
  3. Layer order: wicking top â absorbent core â PUL barrier â outer backing.
  4. Sew with polyester thread and ballpoint needles for knits; 1 cm seam allowance.
  5. Test absorbency with 40 ml water on every 10th pad (or every pad for small batches).
  6. Attach fasteners securely â snap buttons preferred over Velcro for longevity.
  7. Topstitch all edges to prevent fraying and extend product life.
  8. Final inspection: check seams, size, absorbency, and fastener function before packaging.

Further Reading

  • Days for Girls International â Reusable Pad Production Manual (free resources and training materials)
  • UNHCR â Menstrual Hygiene Management: A Guide for Reusable Pad Production (free PDF)
  • WASH Matters â Menstrual Hygiene Management Resources (free toolkits and guides)
  • WHO/UNICEF â Consultation on Draft Long List of Indicators for MHM (free PDF)
  • Menstrual Hygiene Day â Global Advocacy and Resource Hub (free campaign and production materials)

quiz.q: Which fabric is best for the top layer of a reusable pad because it is soft and breathable?
quiz.explanation: Cotton is soft, breathable, and does not irritate the skin, making it ideal for the top layer.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a waterproof backing like PUL?
options: C) To stop liquid from leaking through
quiz.explanation: PUL is a waterproof fabric that prevents leaks while remaining breathable.

quiz.q: Why should you pre-wash fabrics before sewing?
options: B) To shrink them and remove chemicals
quiz.explanation: Pre-washing shrinks the fabric and removes manufacturing chemicals, preventing later shrinkage and irritation.

quiz.q: What is a standard length for a reusable pad for medium flow?
quiz.explanation: A typical medium-flow pad is about 24 cm long, with wings for security.

quiz.q: What material can you use to make a pattern for cutting fabric?
options: B) Cardboard or old X-ray film
quiz.explanation: Cardboard or old X-ray film are durable and can be reused many times.

quiz.q: Why is it important to cut fabric on the grain?
quiz.explanation: Cutting on the grain prevents the fabric from stretching out of shape during sewing and use.

quiz.q: Which stitch is best for finishing edges to prevent fraying?
quiz.explanation: A zigzag stitch encloses the edge and prevents fraying, especially on woven fabrics.

quiz.q: When sewing the pad, why leave a small opening?
options: B) To turn the pad right side out
quiz.explanation: The opening allows you to turn the pad inside out so seams are hidden.

quiz.q: What is the advantage of removable absorbent layers?
options: B) They dry faster and allow adjustable absorbency
D) They are easier to sew
quiz.explanation: Removable layers can be taken out for faster drying and you can add more for heavy flow.

quiz.q: Where should microfiber be placed in a pad?
options: B) In the middle, not against the skin
quiz.explanation: Microfiber absorbs quickly but can irritate skin, so it should be an inner layer.

quiz.q: How much water should a good reusable pad absorb in a test?
quiz.explanation: A standard test is 30 ml (about two tablespoons) to simulate moderate flow.

quiz.q: What is the best fastening method for a reusable pad?
quiz.explanation: Snaps are durable, easy to use, and do not snag like Velcro.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using plastic sheets as a waterproof backing?
options: B) They do not breathe and can cause rashes
D) They are hard to sew
quiz.explanation: Plastic does not allow air flow, leading to sweating and skin irritation.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of topstitching around the pad?
options: B) To reinforce edges and secure layers
quiz.explanation: Topstitching strengthens the edges and keeps all layers flat and secure.

quiz.q: How many washes should a good reusable pad survive?
quiz.explanation: A quality pad should last at least 50 washes with proper care.

quiz.q: What should you check before cutting fabric?
quiz.explanation: Damaged fabric will weaken the pad and may cause leaks.

quiz.q: What is the recommended number of absorbent layers for heavy flow?
quiz.explanation: For heavy flow, use 4 layers to ensure adequate absorption.

quiz.q: Why is polyester thread preferred over cotton thread?
options: B) It is stronger and more durable
quiz.explanation: Polyester thread resists breaking and lasts longer through washing.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a wing on a reusable pad?
options: B) To wrap around underwear and hold the pad in place
quiz.explanation: Wings extend from the sides and fasten around the underwear to prevent shifting.

quiz.q: What should you do if a seam opens when you pull it gently?
options: B) Reinforce with a second stitch
quiz.explanation: Reinforcing the seam ensures the pad does not fall apart during use.

quiz.q: Which fabric is naturally antibacterial and more absorbent than cotton?
quiz.explanation: Bamboo is naturally antibacterial and highly absorbent, though it can be more expensive.

quiz.q: What is the first step in making a pattern?
options: B) Draw the pad shape on paper
quiz.explanation: Drawing the shape on paper allows you to create a template before cutting fabric.

quiz.q: How can you test if a fabric is absorbent?
options: A) Drop water on it and see how fast it absorbs
quiz.explanation: A simple water drop test shows how quickly the fabric absorbs liquid.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a quality control checklist?
options: B) To ensure consistent quality and build trust
quiz.explanation: A checklist helps maintain high standards and customer satisfaction.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid ironing PUL directly?
quiz.explanation: PUL is a synthetic laminate that can melt or be damaged by direct high heat.

quiz.q: What is the best way to dry reusable pads in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Sunlight is a natural disinfectant and helps dry pads quickly, preventing mold.

quiz.q: What should you do if a pad leaks through the backing during a test?
options: B) Use a different backing or add another layer of PUL
quiz.explanation: If the backing leaks, it is not waterproof enough; replace or reinforce it.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of a well-made pad?
options: C) Secure seams and no raw edges
quiz.explanation: Secure seams and finished edges indicate good craftsmanship and durability.

quiz.q: What is the recommended overlap for wings when fastened?
quiz.explanation: At least 2 cm overlap ensures the wings stay fastened securely.

quiz.q: Why is it important to test a sample pad before making many?
options: A) To check fit and comfort
quiz.explanation: Testing helps you adjust the pattern for proper fit and function before mass production.
